conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time to talk with me today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the EPDS) to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply ten questions about the past week, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety, in which case we’ll make a plan together. My goal is to understand how you’re doing and make sure you feel heard and supported. Ready to start?

1. In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*shifts a little in the chair, offers a small smile*

I've been able to laugh sometimes... not as much as I used to before the baby came. Like, my husband made a joke yesterday about how the baby's diaper explosions always happen at the worst times, and I did laugh at that. But mostly... I don't know, things just don't seem as funny anymore. Maybe a couple times this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*nods slowly*

Yeah, like I said… sometimes I can—like with my husband’s joke—but it doesn’t come as easily. I guess I’d say “not so much now,” if that makes sense.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*glances down at my hands in my lap*

I still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when the baby smiles at me—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more… muted. I’ll think “oh, that’ll be nice,” but the spark isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*sighs quietly*

Yeah… I do that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m just not doing a good-enough job as her mom. Last night she wouldn’t sleep after her feeding and I kept wondering what I did wrong—maybe I ate something that upset her stomach, or I didn’t burp her long enough. It’s silly, I know, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings my hands a little*

Sometimes, yeah. Like the other night she was breathing a little fast while she slept, and even after I watched her and counted her breaths and everything seemed fine, I couldn’t shake the worry. My heart was racing and I kept thinking, “What if something’s wrong and I miss it?” It lasted maybe half an hour before I finally dozed off. Most of the time I can talk myself down, but every so often the anxiety just shows up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifts in the chair, hugging my arms*

A couple times... like yesterday when I was walking to the mailbox, my heart just started racing and I felt like I couldn't breathe for a minute. Nothing was wrong - the baby was fine, it was a nice day out - but I had to stop and lean against the wall until it passed. It only lasted a few minutes, but it was scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a small laugh that sounds more tired than amused*

Yeah... I mean, I can usually handle the day-to-day stuff—feeding, changing, trying to nap when she naps—but sometimes it just feels like a lot. Yesterday the dishes piled up, the baby wouldn’t nap unless I held her, and I still hadn’t showered. For a minute I just sat on the couch and thought, “I can’t do all this.” I didn’t cry or anything, but it felt heavy. Then I took a breath, strapped her in the carrier, and got through it, but… yeah, it can feel like too much sometimes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*shakes head slowly*

Not really… I mean, I do get sad here and there, but it hasn’t kept me from sleeping. Most nights once I finally lie down, I drift off pretty fast—exhaustion helps. I might toss and turn for a few minutes if I start replaying the day, but I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy I can’t sleep.”
I have felt sad or miserable

*shrugs a little, voice softer*

Yeah… I guess I do feel kind of down some days. Not every moment, but there’s this lingering sadness that pops up, especially when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels quiet. I’ll look at her and feel happy she’s here, but then this heavy feeling kind of settles in. It’s not all the time—maybe a few times this week—but when it hits, it feels pretty miserable.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*swallows hard, eyes flick toward the window*

Maybe once or twice this week… like two nights ago, she finally went down in her crib and the house was quiet, and I just sat on the couch and started crying. Nothing huge happened—I just felt this wave of “I’m not doing enough” and the tears came. It lasted a few minutes, then I wiped my face and folded the laundry. So, yeah, I’ve cried, but not for hours or anything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—never. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, sure, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom, not… that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms  
- Persistently low mood, “muted” enjoyment, episodic crying (Q2, 8, 9)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Unwarranted worry, nocturnal hyper-vigilance, one acute panic-like episode (Q4, 5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / inadequate coping with daily tasks (Q6)  

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive features with prominent anxiety; sleep is driven by fatigue rather than mood-related insomnia; no anhedonia across all activities.

Risk factors noted  
- Postpartum period (infant ≤ 12 mo)  
- Recurrent guilt / “not a good-enough mom” cognitions  
- Isolated panic symptoms  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (Q10 denies self-harm thoughts)

Screening impression  
Patient endorses multiple DSM-5-TR criteria consistent with probable Perinatal Depression & Anxiety (PHQ-9 estimated ~10–12, GAD-7 indicators moderate). Denies self-harm; no safety concerns at present. Recommends formal diagnostic evaluation and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
